claims.text: What the strip looks like A useful rule of thumb: a normal QT is less than half the preceding RR interval.
claims.quote: A useful rule of thumb is that a normal QT is less than half the preceding RR interval

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Where to measure: lead II or V5, ideally where T waves are most distinct
claims.quote: Measure in lead II or V5, ideally where T waves are most distinct

claims.text: Which lead and beat: usually II or V5–6, but use the lead with the longest measurement; measure several successive beats and take the maximum
claims.quote: The QT interval is usually measured in either lead II or V5-6, however the lead with the longest measurement should be used Several successive beats should be measured, with the maximum interval taken
claims.locator: How to measure the QT interval

claims.text: U waves: include large U waves (> 1 mm) fused to the T wave; exclude smaller U waves and those separate from the T wave
claims.quote: Large U waves (> 1mm) that are fused to the T wave should be included in the measurement Smaller U waves and those that are separate from the T wave should be excluded
claims.locator: How to measure the QT interval

claims.text: Correct for rate: Bazett's formula, QTc = QT / √RR
claims.quote: Must be corrected for rate (QTc) using Bazett's formula: QTc = QT / √ RR.

claims.text: Bazett's limits: over-corrects at rates > 100 bpm and under-corrects at < 60 bpm; adequate from 60 to 100 bpm
claims.quote: It over-corrects at heart rates > 100 bpm and under-corrects at heart rates < 60 bpm, but provides an adequate correction for heart rates ranging from 60 – 100 bpm

claims.text: Outside 60–100 bpm, the Fridericia or Framingham corrections are more accurate and should be used instead
claims.quote: At heart rates outside of the 60 – 100 bpm range, the Fridericia or Framingham corrections are more accurate and should be used instead

claims.text: QTc: normal < 440 ms (men), < 460 ms (women)
claims.quote: Normal QTc: < 440 ms (men), < 460 ms (women)

claims.text: Prolonged QTc: > 440 ms in men or > 460 ms in women
claims.quote: QTc is prolonged if > 440ms in men or > 460ms in women

claims.text: Danger zone: QTc > 500 ms — significant risk of torsades de pointes
claims.quote: Prolonged QTc > 500 ms: significant risk of torsades de pointes

claims.text: Poisoning: with QT-prolonging agents, torsades risk is better described by the absolute (not corrected) QT together with the heart rate on the same tracing, plotted on the QT nomogram
claims.quote: In the context of acute poisoning with QT-prolonging agents, the risk of TdP is better described by the absolute rather than corrected QT. More precisely, the risk of TdP is determined by considering both the absolute QT interval and the simultaneous heart rate (i.e. on the same ECG tracing). These values are then plotted on the QT nomogram (developed by Chan et al) to determine whether the patient is at risk of TdP.

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Mechanism: QT prolongation predisposes to early afterdepolarizations and spatial dispersion of ventricular refractoriness, which can lead to arrhythmias
claims.quote: QT-interval prolongation predisposes to early after-depolarizations and spatial dispersion of ventricular refractoriness, which can lead to arrhythmias.

claims.text: Common causes: congenital long QT syndromes, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, antiarrhythmics (sotalol, amiodarone), antipsychotics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, methadone
claims.quote: Common causes of prolonged QT: congenital long QT syndromes, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, antiarrhythmics (sotalol, amiodarone), antipsychotics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, methadone

claims.text: Other causes: hypothermia, myocardial ischemia, after ROSC from cardiac arrest, raised intracranial pressure
claims.quote: Causes of a prolonged QTc (>440ms) Hypokalaemia Hypomagnesaemia Hypocalcaemia Hypothermia Myocardial ischemia ROSC Post-cardiac arrest Raised intracranial pressure Congenital long QT syndrome Medications/Drugs

claims.text: QT-prolonging medications: the most common predisposing factor for acquired torsades — especially class Ia, Ic or III antiarrhythmics
claims.quote: The most common predisposing factor in acquired TdeP VT is a QT interval–prolonging medication, especially a class Ia, class Ic, or class III antiarrhythmic medication

claims.text: Other medications that can induce torsades: tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines, certain antivirals and antifungals (see CredibleMeds)
claims.quote: Other medications that can induce TdeP VT include tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines, and certain antivirals and antifungals (see CredibleMeds for up-to-date information).

claims.text: In most cases several predisposing causes coexist; they may include female sex, older age, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypothyroidism, and a slow or irregular ventricular rate
claims.quote: In most cases, there are several predisposing causes, which may include (1): Female sex Older age Hypokalemia Hypomagnesemia Hypothyroidism Slow ventricular rate Irregular ventricular rate

claims.text: Hypokalemia: apparent QTc prolongation in the limb leads from T–U fusion, with prominent U waves in the precordial leads
claims.quote: Hypokalaemia causes apparent QTc prolongation in the limb leads (due to T-U fusion) with prominent U waves in the precordial leads.

claims.text: Hypocalcemia: typically prolongs the ST segment, leaving the T wave unchanged
claims.quote: Hypocalcaemia typically prolongs the ST segment, leaving the T wave unchanged

claims.text: Hypothermia (severe): can cause marked QTc prolongation, often with bradyarrhythmias (especially slow AF), Osborn waves and shivering artifact
claims.quote: Severe hypothermia can cause marked QTc prolongation, often in association with bradyarrhythmias (especially slow AF), Osborn waves and shivering artefact

claims.text: Myocardial ischemia: tends to give a modest QTc increase, in the 450–500 ms range
claims.quote: Myocardial ischemia tends to produce a modest increase in the QTc, in the 450-500 ms range

claims.text: This can help separate hyperacute MI from benign early repolarization — both may give similar hyperacute T waves, but BER usually has a normal QTc
claims.quote: This may be useful in distinguishing hyperacute MI from benign early repolarization (both may produce similar hyperacute T waves, but benign early repolarisation (BER) will usually have a normal QTc)

claims.text: Raised ICP (e.g., subarachnoid hemorrhage): a sudden rise may give “cerebral T waves” — widespread, deep T-wave inversions with a prolonged QTc
claims.quote: A sudden rise in intracranial pressure (e.g. due to subarachnoid haemorrhage) may produce characteristic T wave changes (‘cerebral T waves’): widespread, deep T wave inversions with a prolonged QTc

claims.text: Symptoms Long QT syndromes cause no symptoms unless torsades occurs, which can cause palpitations, near-syncope, syncope or sudden death
claims.quote: The LQTS are asymptomatic unless TdP VT occurs, which can cause palpitations, near-syncope, syncope, or sudden death.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Long QT Interval Syndromes

claims.text: Torsades often causes syncope because its rate (200 to 250 beats/minute) is nonperfusing; palpitations are common in conscious patients
claims.quote: TdeP VT often causes syncope because the underlying rate (200 to 250 beats/minute) is nonperfusing. Palpitations are common among patients who are conscious.

claims.text: Treatment Seek and correct electrolyte problems and QT-prolonging medications
claims.quote: Seek and correct electrolytes and QT- prolonging medications.

claims.text: If a medication is the cause, stop it; until it has cleared, frequent or long runs of torsades need the QT shortened by raising the heart rate — temporary pacing, IV isoproterenol, or both are often effective
claims.quote: If a medication is the cause, it is stopped, but until medication clearance is complete, patients with frequent or long runs of TdeP VT require treatment to shorten the QT interval. Because increasing the heart rate shortens the QT interval, temporary pacing, IV isoproterenol, or both are often effective.

claims.text: Torsades: magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 1 to 2 minutes, correction of hypokalemia, pacing or isoproterenol to raise the heart rate, and correction of the cause
claims.quote: The torsades rhythm is treated with magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 1 to 2 minutes, correction of hypokalemia, pacing or isoproterenol to increase heart rate, and correction of the cause.

claims.text: Long term: avoid conditions that prolong the QT; a QTc that stays prolonged after QT-prolonging influences are removed suggests an underlying subclinical congenital long QT syndrome
claims.quote: Long-term treatment is avoidance of conditions that prolong the QT interval. Some patients with an acquired long QT-interval syndrome have an underlying subclinical congenital long QT-interval syndrome suggested by persistent QTc interval prolongation after removal of exogenous QTc prolonging influences (2).

notes.issue: claim widened "a QT interval-prolonging medication" to all medications
